source.title: Self-healing codes: How stable neural populations can track continually reconfiguring neural representations
source.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

confidence_rationale: Every specific assertion in MECH-562's note was checked against the full text and all of them hold verbatim, including the authors' own ansatz disclaimer. The paper is a clean, well-specified simulation in a strong venue; it is a model rather than a measurement, which is the main discount, and its role differs by claim (rival to MECH-553, subject of MECH-562).
failure_signatures: A stable readout can track a continually reconfiguring code using only Hebbian learning plus single-cell homeostasis, with NO external error signal and NO explicit lineage or pairing representation -- so any REE rescue attributed to correctly paired replay must first beat this rival at matched information.

The authors themselves label the coupling of learning rate to homeostatic error an 'ansatz' and a 'prediction that will need to be experimentally confirmed', so the mechanism is not physiologically established and must not be cited as if it were.

The compensation demonstrated is for GRADUAL drift and for abrupt resampling of a few units at a time (plasticity run each time 5 of 100 features changed); it is not a demonstration that receiver-local adaptation handles wholesale representational change.

mapping.source_claim_statement: In a simulated population of 100 encoding units whose tunings drift as a discrete-time Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process (or are abruptly resampled one unit at a time, with plasticity run each time 5 of the 100 features changed), interactions between Hebbian learning and single-cell homeostasis let a readout neuron track the evolving code without external error feedback, by exploiting redundancy in the distributed code. Recurrent feedback of partially stabilised readouts further corrects residual inconsistency.
mapping.ree_translation: For MECH-562 this IS the claim's subject: receiver-local self-healing as the standing rival to every cross-system interface-repair result, producing the same observable (downstream performance restored despite upstream change) with no episodic pair identity, cross-system label or offline replay. For MECH-553 it is the named competitor: if lineage-free estimation matches explicit genealogy at matched information, compressed causal genealogy earns no keep.
mapping.mapping_caveat: A simulation study, not a physiological measurement, and the authors say so. It demonstrates that receiver-local adaptation is SUFFICIENT for a readout to track drift in a redundant code; it does not show that biological circuits do this, nor that a lineage-free estimator can recover DEPENDENCY STRUCTURE between two items -- which is the thing MECH-553 actually claims and this paper never attempts. Per feedback_lit_exp_decoupled it raises no claim's confidence.
mapping.source_context: Computational model; 100 encoding units; OU drift and abrupt per-feature resampling; Hebbian plus single-cell homeostatic plasticity; no external error signal.

confidence_components.notes: PNAS, clearly specified and reproducible; the discount is that it is a model of a mechanism the authors explicitly flag as unconfirmed. Mapping fidelity is high for MECH-562 (the claim is stated about exactly this rule) and lower for MECH-553 (the rival is real but this paper does not test dependency estimation).
